title: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
summary: How DPO turns the RLHF objective into a classification loss on log-prob ratios, why it can overfit or shrink good answers, and how IPO, KTO, ORPO and SimPO change the data, the loss or the reference.
outcomes: Derive the DPO loss from the KL-regularized RLHF objective and explain why the partition function cancels
Compute the DPO loss, implicit rewards and gradient weight for a preference pair from sequence log-probs
Explain why DPO overfits deterministic preferences and how IPO's squared loss keeps the policy near the reference
Compare KTO, ORPO and SimPO by what data, reference model and normalization each needs
Diagnose likelihood displacement and length exploitation and apply fixes such as DPOP or an NLL term

lessons.title: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop

blocks.md: Recall the RLHF recipe from the prerequisite course. First, fit a **reward model** $r_\phi(x, y)$ on human comparisons using the **Bradley-Terry** model: the probability that answer $y_w$ beats $y_l$ for prompt $x$ is $\sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid. Second, run PPO to maximize that reward while a KL penalty keeps the policy near the SFT model.

The DPO paper (Rafailov et al., 2023) calls this pipeline "complex and often unstable". PPO has to **sample** fresh answers from the policy during training, score them with a separate network, and tune many knobs. **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** gets the same optimum from the same preference data with a single classification-style loss and no sampling during fine-tuning. This lesson shows why that is possible.

blocks.title: Two routes from preference pairs to an aligned model

scenes.caption: Classic RLHF: preferences train a reward model, then PPO optimizes the policy against it with a KL penalty to the SFT model.
The expensive part: every PPO step generates new answers from the current policy and scores them, so training includes slow autoregressive sampling.
DPO: the same preference pairs and the same SFT starting point feed one loss on log-probabilities. No separate reward network, no sampling during training.

blocks.md: Both routes start from the same goal, the KL-regularized objective. Here $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the **reference policy** (the frozen SFT model) and $\beta$ sets how strongly the policy is held near it:

blocks.caption: The RLHF objective (DPO paper Eq. 3). Large beta: stay close to the reference. Small beta: chase reward.

blocks.md: This objective has a known closed-form maximizer: take the reference distribution and reweight every answer by $\exp(r/\beta)$, then renormalize. The normalizer $Z(x)$ is a sum over **every possible answer** to $x$, which is why nobody computes it for a real language model.

blocks.tex: \pi^*(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\, \exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\Big), \quad Z(x) = \sum_{y} \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\Big)
blocks.caption: DPO paper Eq. 4.

blocks.md: Make it concrete with a toy prompt that has only three possible answers A, B and C. The reference model gives them 50%, 30% and 20%. A reward model scores them 1.0, 2.0 and 0.0. So B is best, but the reference prefers A.

blocks.prompt: At $\beta = 0.25$ (weak KL leash), roughly how much probability does the optimal policy put on B, which starts at 30%?
blocks.reveal: About **97%**. Reweighting multiplies B by $e^{2/0.25} = e^8$ and A by only $e^{4}$, so B dominates: 2.96% A, 97.02% B, 0.02% C. The animation below shows how the optimum slides from the reference toward the best answer as $\beta$ shrinks.

blocks.title: Optimal policy for the toy prompt as beta shrinks

scenes.caption: beta = 10: a strong leash. The optimum is almost the reference: 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%.
beta = 1: B overtakes A. 36.0%, 58.71%, 5.3%. The policy moves mass toward reward but still respects the reference.
beta = 0.5: 18.22%, 80.79%, 0.99%. The worst answer C is almost gone.
beta = 0.25: 2.96%, 97.02%, 0.02%. As beta goes to 0 the optimum collapses onto the single highest-reward answer.

blocks.md: Now the key algebra. Take the log of the closed form and solve for the reward:

blocks.caption: DPO paper Eq. 5: any reward can be written through its own optimal policy.

blocks.md: The troublesome $Z(x)$ depends only on the prompt, not on the answer. Bradley-Terry only ever uses a **difference** of two rewards for the same prompt, so $\beta \log Z(x)$ cancels. Check it in the toy at $\beta = 1$: $\beta \log(\pi^*/\pi_{\text{ref}})$ is -0.329 for A, 0.671 for B and -1.329 for C. Each is the true reward minus the same constant 1.329, so B minus A is still exactly 1.0.

blocks.tex: p(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\!\Big(\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)
blocks.caption: DPO paper Eq. 6: human preferences written using only policies, no reward network.

blocks.md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

blocks.question: Why can DPO ignore the partition function $Z(x)$, which sums over every possible response?
options: It is always equal to 1 for a normalized language model
It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the reward difference that Bradley-Terry uses
DPO estimates it with Monte Carlo samples from the policy
It is absorbed into the learning rate
blocks.explain: $\beta \log Z(x)$ is the same for every answer to a given prompt. Bradley-Terry compares two answers to the same prompt through $r(y_w) - r(y_l)$, so the term cancels exactly. No sampling or approximation is needed.

blocks.question: In the toy example, what happens to the optimal policy as $\beta$ grows very large?
options: It approaches the reference distribution: 50%, 30%, 20%
It puts all mass on B, the highest reward
It becomes uniform over A, B and C
It puts all mass on A, the reference's favorite
blocks.explain: Reweighting by $\exp(r/\beta)$ approaches multiplying everything by 1 as $\beta$ grows, so the optimum returns to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. At $\beta = 10$ it is already 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%. Small $\beta$ is what collapses it onto B.

lessons.title: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers

blocks.md: Replace $\pi^*$ in the preference formula with a trainable policy $\pi_\theta$ and maximize the likelihood of the observed human choices. That gives the DPO loss: a binary logistic loss whose logit is the gap between two **implicit rewards**.

blocks.caption: DPO paper Eq. 7. y_w is the chosen (winning) response, y_l the rejected (losing) one.

blocks.md: Each $\log \pi(y\mid x)$ is a **sequence log-probability**: the sum of the per-token log-probs of the response, with prompt tokens masked out exactly as in SFT. One training step therefore needs four numbers per pair: policy and reference log-probs for the chosen and rejected responses. The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT model and the policy starts as an identical copy, so at step 0 every log-ratio is 0.
A tiny pair: the prompt is "Capital of France?", the chosen answer is "It is Paris." and the rejected answer is "It is Lyon." (4 tokens each, made-up but consistent log-probs).

blocks.title: Token log-probs for one pair, before and after training

scenes.caption: Reference model (and the policy at step 0). Sum the response tokens: log p(y_w) = -2.8 and log p(y_l) = -4.3. The reference already prefers Paris.
The first two tokens are identical in both answers with identical context, so their log-probs cancel in the chosen-minus-rejected difference. Only tokens from the first difference onward matter.
Policy after some DPO steps: Paris rises from -0.9 to -0.5, Lyon falls from -2.1 to -3.0, and the period after Lyon drifts to -0.7.
New sums: policy log p(y_w) = -2.4 and log p(y_l) = -5.3. Compared with the reference, chosen gained 0.4 nats and rejected lost 1.0 nat.

blocks.md: Now the loss with $\beta = 0.1$, the default in the DPO paper and in Hugging Face TRL. The **implicit reward** of each answer is $\beta$ times its policy-to-reference log-ratio: chosen $0.1 \times 0.4 = 0.04$, rejected $0.1 \times (-1.0) = -0.10$. The **margin** is $0.04 - (-0.10) = 0.14$, so the loss is $-\log \sigma(0.14) = 0.6256$, down from $\ln 2 = 0.6931$ at step 0, where the margin was 0.

blocks.title: Tracing the DPO loss on the pair above
blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def dpo_loss(pi_w, pi_l, ref_w, ref_l, beta=0.1):
    # each input: summed log-prob of a response (prompt tokens masked)
    pi_logratios = pi_w - pi_l
    ref_logratios = ref_w - ref_l
    logits = beta * (pi_logratios - ref_logratios)
    losses = -F.logsigmoid(logits)
    chosen_reward = beta * (pi_w - ref_w).detach()
    rejected_reward = beta * (pi_l - ref_l).detach()
    return losses, chosen_reward, rejected_reward

scenes.caption: Inputs are four sequence log-probs from the trained policy and the frozen reference (sums from the previous figure).
The policy prefers chosen by 2.9 nats; the reference already preferred it by 1.5 nats.
Only the improvement over the reference counts: 2.9 - 1.5 = 1.4 nats, scaled by beta to a logit of 0.14.
Binary logistic loss on that logit. A margin of 0 gives ln 2 = 0.6931; this pair is at 0.6256.
The implicit rewards are logged for monitoring, detached from the graph. Their difference is the margin 0.14.

blocks.md: What does a gradient step do? The paper's gradient has a clear reading: push up the chosen log-prob, push down the rejected one, and **weight** the whole pair by how wrong the implicit reward model currently is.

blocks.caption: Where the implicit reward is beta times the log-ratio to the reference.

blocks.md: For our pair the weight is $\sigma(-0.14) = 0.4651$, a little below the 0.5 it had at step 0. A pair the model already ranks correctly by a wide margin gets almost no gradient; a pair it ranks backwards gets nearly full weight. Drag $\beta$ in the figure to see how it rescales the margin axis.

blocks.title: DPO loss and per-pair weight versus log-ratio gap

scenes.caption: beta = 0.1. Our pair (gap 1.4 nats) sits near the middle: loss 0.6256, weight 0.4651. Pairs ranked backwards (negative gap) get weight near 1.
beta = 0.5: the same gap counts five times more. A 5-nat gap already drives the loss to 0.0789 and the weight to 0.0759, so learning on that pair stops sooner.
beta = 0.02: the curves flatten. The policy must move much further from the reference before a pair counts as solved.

blocks.md: The weight $\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$ is what makes DPO work. The authors report that a naive version without this weighting (push chosen up, rejected down, equally on every pair) can make the language model degenerate.

How to pick $\beta$: the DPO paper used 0.1 for most experiments and 0.5 for TL;DR summarization, and TRL defaults to 0.1. TRL documents it as controlling deviation from the reference: higher $\beta$ means less deviation.

The paper reports DPO matching or beating PPO-based RLHF on its tasks: on TL;DR summarization DPO reached about a 61% GPT-4 win rate against reference summaries at temperature 0, versus 57% for PPO at its best temperature, and it was more robust to sampling temperature.

blocks.question: At step 0 the policy equals the reference. What is the DPO loss of every pair, and what is each pair's gradient weight?
options: Loss 0 and weight 0, since nothing has changed
Loss 1 and weight 1
It depends on how strongly the reference prefers y_w
Loss ln 2 (about 0.693) and weight 0.5
blocks.explain: All log-ratios are 0, so the margin is 0 for every pair regardless of the reference's own preference. $-\log \sigma(0) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ and the weight is $\sigma(0) = 0.5$. The reference's preference cancels because DPO only scores improvement over the reference.

blocks.question: A pair has policy log-probs chosen -30, rejected -20 and reference log-probs chosen -32, rejected -18, with $\beta = 0.1$. What is the DPO margin, and does the implicit reward rank the pair correctly?
options: -1.0, ranked wrong, because the policy gives the chosen answer lower probability
+0.4, ranked correctly, even though the policy still gives the chosen answer lower probability
+1.0, ranked correctly
0, because the reference and policy disagree
blocks.explain: Chosen log-ratio: -30 - (-32) = +2. Rejected: -20 - (-18) = -2. Margin 0.1 x (2 - (-2)) = +0.4, so the implicit reward ranks it correctly. Yet the policy itself still prefers the rejected text (-20 beats -30). DPO scores improvement relative to the reference, not raw likelihood; lesson 5 shows why this matters.

lessons.title: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds

blocks.md: Bradley-Terry turns a reward gap into a probability with a sigmoid. Run it backwards and a preference probability of exactly 1 needs an **infinite** reward gap. Azar et al. (2023), the IPO paper, point out that this is the normal case in practice: most prompts appear with one labeled pair, so the empirical preference is 1 even when the true probability is, say, 0.8.

In DPO the reward is $\beta$ times a log-ratio, so an infinite reward gap means an infinite log-ratio: the rejected answer's probability is driven to 0 **whatever $\beta$ is**. The KL leash that $\beta$ was supposed to provide stops binding. Classic RLHF dodges some of this because the reward model is regularized and underfit; DPO has no separate reward model to underfit.

The IPO paper's own toy example makes this precise: two possible answers, a uniform reference (50% each), and data in which $y_1$ always beats $y_2$. The paper solves this case in closed form; we rerun it as a simplified simulation: plain gradient descent (learning rate 0.1) on the two logits of a softmax policy.

blocks.prompt: Set the regularization strength high: $\beta = \tau = 1$. After 10,000 steps, where is DPO's probability on $y_1$: near 62%, near 73%, or near 100%?
blocks.reveal: Near **100%** (99.95%). DPO's loss keeps rewarding a larger gap forever; the gradient only shrinks, never reverses. IPO with the same $\tau = 1$ stops at 62.25%, the value its closed form predicts. The figure below compares several strengths.

blocks.title: Probability of y1 during training, two-answer toy

scenes.caption: Step 10. Everything starts at 50%. IPO moves fast toward its target; DPO is still climbing.
Step 100. IPO has settled at 99.33%, 73.11% and 62.25%: stronger regularization (larger tau) keeps it closer to the 50% reference.
Step 1,000. DPO is at 99.96%, 99.96% and 99.49%. Its regularization strength changes only how fast it gets there.
Step 10,000. DPO is above 99.9% for every tau (99.95% at tau = 1) and still rising. IPO has not moved since step 100.

blocks.md: IPO (Identity Preference Optimization) comes from a general family the paper calls $\Psi$PO. DPO is the member with $\Psi(q) = \log\frac{q}{1-q}$, which is unbounded as $q \to 1$. IPO uses the identity, which is bounded. For a dataset of pairs, the resulting loss is a plain **regression**: push the log-ratio gap $h$ toward a fixed target $\frac{1}{2\tau}$, no further.

blocks.tex: h_\pi(y_w, y_l) = \log \frac{\pi(y_w\mid x)\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}{\pi(y_l\mid x)\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{IPO}} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(h_\pi(y_w,y_l) - \frac{1}{2\tau}\Big)^2\Big]
blocks.caption: IPO paper Eq. 17 and Algorithm 1. tau plays the role of DPO's beta.

blocks.md: In the two-answer toy the reference is uniform, so $h$ is just the logit gap and the optimum is $\pi(y_1) = \sigma\big(\frac{1}{2\tau}\big)$: 62.25% at $\tau = 1$, 73.11% at $\tau = 0.5$, 99.33% at $\tau = 0.1$. That matches the simulation exactly. Slide $\tau$ below.

blocks.title: Where each method converges in the two-answer toy

scenes.caption: IPO's optimum moves smoothly from near-deterministic (small tau) back to the 50% reference (large tau). tau is a real dial.
DPO's optimum is a flat line at 1: with a deterministic preference, beta cannot hold the policy near the reference.

blocks.md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

In TRL, IPO is `loss_type="ipo"` in `DPOConfig`, and the `beta` argument is then IPO's $\tau$. The squared loss also pushes back if a pair overshoots the target gap, which the logistic loss never does.

blocks.question: With IPO at $\tau = 0.25$ in the two-answer toy, what probability does the policy converge to on $y_1$?
options: 50%, the reference
About 73%
About 88%
blocks.explain: The target gap is $1/(2\tau) = 2$, so $\pi(y_1) = \sigma(2) \approx 0.881$. Smaller $\tau$ means a bigger target gap and a more confident policy, but never fully deterministic.

blocks.question: Why does DPO's regularization fail on a pair that appears once in the data?
options: Because DPO forgets to load the reference model
Because the empirical preference for that pair is 1, and fitting probability 1 with a sigmoid needs an unbounded log-ratio gap regardless of beta
Because beta is too large by default
Because the gradient weight grows as the margin grows
blocks.explain: One label means the observed preference is 1. The logistic loss can always be lowered further by widening the gap, so the optimum sits at infinity and beta only changes the speed. The weight actually shrinks with the margin; that slows drift but never stops it.

lessons.title: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs

blocks.md: DPO and IPO need **pairs**: two answers to the same prompt plus a judgment of which is better. Much real feedback is not like that; it is a single answer marked good or bad. **KTO** (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization, Ethayarajh et al., 2024) learns from that binary signal and, the authors report, matches or beats preference-based methods at scales from 1B to 30B parameters.

The idea comes from prospect theory: people judge an outcome relative to a **reference point**, and losses loom larger than equal gains. KTO uses the same implicit reward as DPO without $\beta$, $r_\theta(x,y) = \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, and asks a different question: is this answer's reward above or below a reference point $z_0$?

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{KTO}} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y}\big[\lambda_y - v(x,y)\big], \quad v(x,y) = \begin{cases} \lambda_D\, \sigma\big(\beta (r_\theta(x,y) - z_0)\big) & y \text{ desirable} \\ \lambda_U\, \sigma\big(\beta (z_0 - r_\theta(x,y))\big) & y \text{ undesirable} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: KTO paper Eq. 8. lambda_D and lambda_U weight desirable and undesirable examples.

blocks.md: The reference point is meant to be $z_0 = \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}})$, how far the policy has moved overall. Sampling from the policy to measure that is slow, so KTO uses a cheap, biased estimate: within a microbatch of $m$ examples, pair each prompt with the **next example's** output, average those log-ratios, and clamp at 0. It is not backpropagated; it only sets where the loss saturates.

blocks.title: Estimating the KTO reference point in a microbatch of 4

scenes.caption: Four unpaired examples. D marks a desirable output, U an undesirable one. Each prompt has exactly one answer; no pairs anywhere.
Shift outputs by one: x1 with y2, x2 with y3, and so on. Mismatched pairs avoid outputs that were hand-picked as canonically good or bad, which have unusually large rewards.
Policy-vs-reference log-ratios on the mismatched pairs: 0.3, -0.1, 0.5, 0.1. Mean 0.2, clamp at 0 leaves it: z0 = 0.2.
Each example's own log-ratio is compared to z0 = 0.2. y1 (1.0) and y2 (-0.5) are on the right side; y3 (0.1) is a desirable output below z0, and y4 (0.6) is an undesirable output above it.

blocks.md: Per-example losses with $\lambda_D = \lambda_U = 1$. We use $\beta = 1$ first so the differences are easy to see; the paper's default is $\beta = 0.1$.

scenes.caption: beta = 1: losses 0.31, 0.3318, 0.525, 0.5987. The two examples on the wrong side of z0 (y3, y4) carry the largest loss and the largest gradient.
beta = 0.1 (default): 0.48, 0.4825, 0.5025, 0.51. Same ordering, but every example sits near the middle of the sigmoid, where it is steep and nothing is saturated yet.

blocks.title: KTO loss as a function of an example's log-ratio

scenes.caption: Desirable outputs want r above z0, undesirable ones below it. Far from z0 each curve flattens: the loss saturates and that example stops pulling.
If the policy drifts everywhere, z0 rises (here to 2). A desirable output must now beat the overall drift, not just the reference, so blunt across-the-board increases earn nothing.
beta = 0.1: very gentle slopes. The KTO paper ties beta to risk aversion and recommends 0.1 as a default, with smaller values when the model was already fine-tuned on the same data.

blocks.md: The $\lambda$ weights handle class imbalance. The paper recommends choosing them so that $\frac{\lambda_D n_D}{\lambda_U n_U} \in [1, \frac{3}{2}]$, where $n_D$ and $n_U$ count desirable and undesirable examples. With one desirable example for every 10 undesirable ones, set $\lambda_U = 1$ and $\lambda_D$ between 10 and 15. The authors also find KTO wants a learning rate 2x to 10x higher than DPO, since its rewards are smaller in magnitude, and a microbatch of at least 2 so $z_0$ can be estimated.

KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

blocks.question: Your feedback log has 2,000 thumbs-up and 20,000 thumbs-down responses. Following the KTO paper's guidance with $\lambda_U = 1$, which $\lambda_D$ is in range?
options: 0.1, to down-weight the rare class
1, the default
blocks.explain: The ratio $\lambda_D n_D / (\lambda_U n_U)$ should land in [1, 1.5]. With $n_D/n_U = 0.1$, $\lambda_D$ must be between 10 and 15, so 12 fits. Leaving it at 1 lets the undesirable class dominate the gradient.

blocks.question: Why does KTO estimate $z_0$ from mismatched (prompt, other example's output) pairs instead of each example's own output?
options: Because own outputs are usually chosen to be clearly good or bad, so their rewards are unrepresentatively large
Because mismatched pairs need no forward pass
Because the own output's log-ratio is always zero
Because it makes the estimate unbiased
blocks.explain: The paper says matched outputs have often been deliberately picked as canonically good or bad, giving high-magnitude rewards that would skew the reference point. The mismatched estimate still costs an extra forward pass and is explicitly biased (clamping adds upward bias), but it is cheap and stable.

lessons.title: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model

blocks.md: Every method so far keeps a frozen reference model: DPO, IPO and KTO all need $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ log-probs for every response. That is a second copy of the model in memory, or an extra precomputation pass. SimPO's authors measured that removing it cut run time by roughly 20% and GPU memory by about 10% versus a vanilla DPO implementation.

TRL's `DPOTrainer` can also precompute reference log-probs once with `precompute_ref_log_probs=True`, which pays the reference cost up front instead of on every step. Reference-free methods remove it entirely.

**ORPO** (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization, Hong et al., 2024) starts from an observation about SFT. Fine-tuning OPT-350M on only the chosen answers from Anthropic HH, they saw the log-probs of the **rejected** answers rise right along with the chosen ones: cross-entropy never penalizes unwanted outputs. ORPO adds a penalty to the SFT loss so one stage does both jobs, starting from the base model with no separate SFT stage and no reference model.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{ORPO}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} + \lambda\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{OR}}, \quad \mathcal{L}_{\text{OR}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\log \frac{\text{odds}_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\text{odds}_\theta(y_l\mid x)}\Big), \quad \text{odds}_\theta(y\mid x) = \frac{P_\theta(y\mid x)}{1 - P_\theta(y\mid x)}
blocks.caption: ORPO paper Eqs. 4 to 7. P is the exponential of the average per-token log-prob, not the full sequence probability.

blocks.md: Worked numbers: chosen average token log-prob -0.5 gives $P = 0.6065$ and odds 1.5415; rejected -0.9 gives $P = 0.4066$ and odds 0.6851. The log odds ratio is $0.4328 - (-0.3782) = 0.8109$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\text{OR}} = -\log\sigma(0.8109) = 0.3677$. With the chosen NLL of 0.5 and $\lambda = 0.1$, the total is $0.5 + 0.0368 = 0.5368$. The paper used $\lambda$ between 0.1 and 0.25 depending on the model.

**SimPO** (Simple Preference Optimization, Meng et al., 2024) attacks a different mismatch. DPO's reward is a log-ratio to the reference, but generation is guided by the policy's own likelihood. The authors found that after DPO training only about 50% of training triples had the chosen answer ranked above the rejected one by average log-likelihood. SimPO makes the reward the policy's **average** token log-prob, scaled by $\beta$, and asks it to win by a **target margin** $\gamma$.

blocks.caption: SimPO paper Eq. 6. |y| is the response length in tokens.

blocks.md: Why average instead of sum? Summed log-probs fall with length, so they penalize long answers. Take a 120-token chosen answer averaging -0.8 nats per token and a 40-token rejected one averaging -1.1.

blocks.title: Summed versus length-normalized scores for one pair

scenes.caption: Summed negative log-likelihood: 96 versus 44 nats (lower is more likely). By total probability the short rejected answer looks far better.
Per-token average: 0.8 versus 1.1 nats. Normalized, the chosen answer is the more fluent one, matching the label.
SimPO rewards with beta = 2.5 are 2.5 x (-0.8) = -2.0 and 2.5 x (-1.1) = -2.75 (shown as magnitudes). Gap 0.75, then gamma is subtracted.

blocks.md: With $\beta = 2.5$ and $\gamma = 1.0$ (the paper suggests $\beta$ of 2.0 to 2.5 and $\gamma$ of 0.5 to 1.5) the logit is $0.75 - 1.0 = -0.25$ and the loss is 0.8259. Although the chosen answer already ranks first, it does not clear the margin, so SimPO keeps pushing. With $\gamma = 0$ the same pair would score a loss of 0.3869. The paper found that win rate first rises then falls as $\gamma$ grows: too large a margin degrades generation.

scenes.caption: DPO and IPO: the same inputs (pairs plus reference), different loss shape: logistic versus squared regression to a target gap.
KTO keeps the reference but drops pairing: unpaired good or bad examples are enough.
ORPO and SimPO drop the reference model. ORPO folds in the SFT loss so alignment happens in one stage; SimPO uses a length-normalized reward plus a margin.

blocks.md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every offline method, DPO included.

blocks.question: For the SimPO pair above ($\beta = 2.0$, $\gamma = 0.5$), what is the logit inside the sigmoid?
blocks.explain: Rewards are 2.0 x (-0.8) = -1.6 and 2.0 x (-1.1) = -2.2. Gap 0.6, minus $\gamma = 0.5$, gives 0.1 (loss 0.6444). 52 is the summed-log-prob gap, which length normalization exists to avoid.

blocks.question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
blocks.explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

lessons.title: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes

blocks.md: Back to a fact from lesson 2: the DPO loss sees only the **difference** between the chosen and rejected log-ratios. Nothing in it says the chosen answer must become more likely. Pal et al. (2024, the Smaug paper) show the loss can be lowered while the chosen answer's likelihood falls below the reference, as long as the rejected one falls faster.

blocks.prompt: With $\beta = 0.3$, which state has lower DPO loss: (a) chosen log-ratio -2, rejected -8 (both less likely than before), or (b) chosen +1, rejected -1?
blocks.reveal: **(a)**. Its margin is 0.3 x 6 = 1.8 (loss 0.153) versus 0.3 x 2 = 0.6 (loss 0.4375) for (b). DPO happily prefers a model that made its good answer **less** likely, because the gap is wider.

blocks.title: DPO versus DPOP on two training states (beta 0.3)

scenes.caption: Plain DPO loss: 0.153 for (a) and 0.4375 for (b). Gradient descent moves toward state (a), where the preferred answer lost likelihood.
DPOP adds a penalty of lambda x max(0, log ref/policy on y_w) inside the logit. With lambda = 50 (the paper's setting) state (a) costs 28.2 while (b) is unchanged at 0.4375.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPOP}} = -\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\log \sigma\Big(\beta\Big(\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)} - \lambda \max\Big(0, \log \frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}\Big)\Big)\Big)\Big]
blocks.caption: DPO-Positive (Smaug paper Eq. 3). The penalty is zero while the chosen answer stays at least as likely as under the reference.

blocks.md: The Smaug paper pinpoints when this bites: pairs with a small **edit distance**, like "2+2=4" versus "2+2=5". Tokens before the difference cancel, and their analysis shows the gradient on the tokens **after** the differing one tends to lower the probability of the correct token, so the whole tail of the good answer gets less likely. Our Paris and Lyon pair from lesson 2 is exactly this shape.

A second failure is **length exploitation**. Park et al. (2024) found that preference datasets show only a small bias toward longer answers (Anthropic HH: 79.6 versus 75.7 tokens mean for preferred versus dispreferred), yet unregularized DPO models produced answers about twice as long on average, far outside the data. Their fix adds $\alpha(|y_w| - |y_l|)$ to the DPO logit, so a longer chosen answer needs less implicit reward to count as a win. SimPO's length normalization from lesson 5 targets the same bias.

Watch the logged implicit rewards, not just the loss. TRL logs `rewards/chosen`, `rewards/rejected`, `rewards/margins` and `rewards/accuracies`. A rising margin with `rewards/chosen` steadily going negative is the likelihood-displacement pattern above, and growing output length is the second warning sign.

How is DPO used in a frontier recipe? The Llama 3 paper (2024) aligns its models in several rounds, each being SFT then DPO. The team says they also explored on-policy algorithms such as PPO but found DPO needed less compute for large models and performed better, especially on instruction following. Their DPO details: $\beta = 0.1$; preference data mostly from the latest batches collected with the best models of the previous round, so it stays close to the policy being trained; and two changes to the loss.

scenes.caption: Round 1: collect human preferences, train a reward model (used for rejection sampling to pick the best of K samples as SFT data), then SFT and DPO. Schematic: block lengths are not real durations.
Round 2: new preferences are sampled from the best round-1 models, so DPO trains on data close to the current policy. This is how an offline method gets some of the benefit of on-policy RL.

blocks.md:
The two loss changes map directly onto this lesson's failure modes:

1. **Mask formatting tokens** (headers, termination tokens) in both chosen and rejected answers. Tokens common to both get pushed up and down at once; the team saw tail repetition and abrupt end-of-turn tokens without this mask.
2. **Add an NLL term** with coefficient 0.2 on the chosen sequences, citing the DPOP paper among others, to keep formatting and stop the chosen log-prob from falling.

Choosing among the variants: DPO is the default for paired data with an SFT model. Use IPO-style or early-stopped training when labels are near-deterministic and you need to stay close to the reference; KTO when feedback is unpaired or imbalanced; ORPO or SimPO when a reference model is too costly. Whatever you choose, keep the chosen likelihood and output length under watch.

blocks.question: During DPO training your margin and reward accuracy climb steadily, but `rewards/chosen` keeps getting more negative and outputs drift toward degenerate repetitions. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Lower beta so the model can move further from the reference
Add a term that keeps the chosen log-prob up, such as DPOP's penalty or an NLL loss on chosen answers
Train more epochs so the margin saturates
Remove the reference model to save memory
blocks.explain: The pattern is likelihood displacement: the gap widens because both answers fall. DPOP's hinge penalty and Llama 3's NLL term (coefficient 0.2) both directly penalize a falling chosen log-prob. Lowering beta or training longer lets drift continue.

blocks.question: Why might DPO on preference data collected from an old model work worse than DPO on fresh pairs sampled from the current best model?
options: The implicit reward is only trained on responses near the data, so pairs far from the current policy say little about what it actually generates
DPO cannot read old data formats
Old data always has longer answers
Fresh data removes the need for a reference model
blocks.explain: DPO is offline: it only shapes probabilities on the responses in the dataset. If those come from a different distribution than the policy, much of what the policy generates is never scored. Llama 3 collected each round's data with the best recent models for this reason, so the training data better matches the policy being optimized.
